records.claim: Adding a small, measured amount of fermentable ('priming') sugar to beer immediately before sealing it into bottles triggers a renewed, small-scale fermentation inside each sealed bottle. Because the CO2 produced by that renewed fermentation has no other escape path, it dissolves into the beer under the pressure that builds inside the sealed bottle, carbonating it. The amount of priming sugar needed depends on the specific beer (its existing dissolved CO2, temperature, style) and the carbonation level wanted -- there is no single universal number that applies to every batch.

records.claim: Diacetyl is a compound associated with a butter or butterscotch aroma and flavour in beer. During normal fermentation, yeast releases a precursor that turns into diacetyl in the beer, and healthy yeast can take diacetyl back up and convert it into compounds with little flavour; this depends on the beer staying in contact with enough yeast during fermentation and maturation. Certain lactic acid bacteria can also produce diacetyl. Low levels can be accepted in some beer styles, but diacetyl is generally undesirable when it is unintentionally prominent.

sources.ref: Sutea C.M., Mudura E., Pop C.R., Salanta L.C., Farcas A.C., Balas P.C., Gal E. et al., Beer Aroma Compounds: Key Odorants, Off-Flavour Compounds and Improvement Proposals, Foods 14(24):4287, 2025, DOI 10.3390/foods14244287 -- PMC12732517 via Europe PMC full-text XML (accessed 2026-10-01)
sources.note: Issue #464 source gate: DMS 'sweetcorn, cooked vegetable' odour; oxidised/aged/stale and trans-2-nonenal 'cardboard, papery'; acetaldehyde 'green apples or unripe apples'; MBT 'skunky' odour. Only descriptor wording is used; the review's thresholds, mechanisms and corrective actions are NOT carried. mdpi.com returned 403, so the text was read via Europe PMC.

records.notes: Sensory S-4 (documented_fact, issue #467; source gate #464 accepted by Chief). The claim contains no numbers, thresholds, times or temperatures. DESCRIPTOR != DIAGNOSIS is a notes/methodology/teaching boundary and is deliberately NOT asserted as a factual sentence in the claim: no opened source states it as a sentence; it is supported only indirectly (TCA also smells of wet cardboard; skunkiness is commonly misattributed to staling and many compounds contribute to stale flavour; acetaldehyde character changes with concentration). Teaching must keep 'this smells like X' separate from 'this is compound Y' or 'this was caused by Z'. OWNERSHIP: DMS process truth stays with FACT-BOIL-0002; oxidation process truth stays with FACT-OXY-0002; the light-struck mechanism stays with future S-3; acetaldehyde gets descriptor vocabulary ONLY (no maturation, immaturity, cause, yeast-health or process claim); sulphur is not part of S-4. Deliberately NOT claimed: any threshold or concentration; any fixed process time or temperature; that cooked corn proves a short boil; that cardboard proves oxygen pickup; that green apple proves immature beer; that skunky proves one specific packaging error or that skunky means stale; any precursor, boil, oxygen, light, hop, riboflavin or glass content; a broad off-flavour catalogue (extra descriptors such as cabbage, tinned tomato, cucumber, black currant, latex paint, cat or foxy are not carried). Sherry-like is OMITTED by Chief decision (Tier B-only support) and remains a teaching note only. SOURCE LIMITATIONS: the two Tier A sources are both MDPI reviews (same publisher); no ASBC/EBC flavour-terminology standard or flavour wheel was opened; Oxford text was read via a hosted reproduction and its oxidation entry was truncated; the Brewers Association DMS article is members-only and only its public summary line was seen; Kunze DMS/aldehyde pages are OCR-only and not cited; individual sensitivity/anosmia differences are not sourced and not needed. SOURCE-ACCESS LIMITATIONS: this Bridge run did not reopen the sources; the record encodes the Chief-accepted wording and the source evidence recorded and accepted on issue #464 (access date 2026-10-01), whose URLs are carried in the source refs.

records.claim: Sourness can be an intended part of a beer: sour beer styles are deliberately made acidic, for example with lactic acid bacteria or mixed microbial cultures. In a beer that was not meant to be sour, unexpected sourness can be associated with unwanted microbial contamination that spoils the beer's flavour.

sources.type: peer-reviewed review (Frontiers in Microbiology, CC BY) -- independent Tier A anchor
sources.ref: Bouchez A., De Vuyst L., Acetic Acid Bacteria in Sour Beer Production: Friend or Foe?, Front. Microbiol. 13:957167, 2022, DOI 10.3389/fmicb.2022.957167 -- PMC9386357 via Europe PMC full text (accessed 2026-10-01)
sources.note: Issue #468 source gate: controlled growth gives a desirable acidic flavour in sour beers; for almost all other beers bacteria are undesirable because of spoilage potential, and acetic acid bacteria spoilage is characterised by a sour taste and vinegary aroma. Organism lists and process detail in the review are NOT carried.

records.notes: Sensory S-2 (documented_fact, issue #470; source gate #468 accepted by Chief). The claim contains no numbers, pH values or thresholds, and no organism names. TASTE ALONE DOES NOT ESTABLISH THE CAUSE is a notes/methodology/teaching boundary and is deliberately NOT asserted as a factual sentence in the claim (Chief decision on #468): no opened source states it as one sentence; it is supported only indirectly (more than one route to acidity, including acetic acid via acetaldehyde oxidation or acetic acid bacteria, and lactic acid from some yeasts without bacteria; organisms are identified by laboratory methods). Teaching may say that sourness shows only that the beer is more sour than intended. The yeast-souring example from the #468 proposal is NOT carried because its support (Osburn et al. 2018) is abstract-only. Deliberately NOT claimed: any health or safety statement in either direction (no 'undrinkable', 'unsafe' or 'safe'; 'spoils the flavour' is a quality phrase only); that sour means infected; that all sour beers are spoiled; any organism catalogue; any pH, acidity number or threshold; diagnostic certainty (a vinegar smell does not prove acetic acid bacteria); treatment, rescue, pasteurisation or sanitation advice; 'infection' as the default word (use 'unwanted microbial contamination' and 'spoilage'). FACT-COOL-0001/0003 and FACT-SAFE-* keep their own scope. SOURCE LIMITATIONS: A2 and A3 are both MDPI reviews (same publisher), A1 (Frontiers) is the independent Tier A anchor; Kunze is industrial scope, a local scan of unofficial provenance, and was inspected as a page image not OCR; no Tier A sensory/consumer source separates normal beer acidity from noticeable sourness; Osburn et al. 2018 (abstract only) and the members-only Brewers Association lactic-acid page were not cited; no health evidence was sought or used. SOURCE-ACCESS LIMITATIONS: this Bridge run did not reopen the sources; the record encodes the Chief-accepted wording and the source evidence recorded and accepted on issue #468 (access date 2026-10-01), whose references are carried in the source refs.
